catalog_quote: p.53: "Phonologically, Khamti word boundaries or morpheme boundaries are primarily defined by tones. Every syllable consisting of wide range of combinations V, VV, CV, VC, CVC, CVV, CVVC, CCVC are marked by tones and are mono-morphemic. However, this is not true in case of loan words where the language adapts its tonal feature to every syllable of a non-monomorphemic word. ... Generally, the first word component of disyllabic nouns undergoes consonant deletion, vowel harmony or consonantal assimilation with the second syllable or second word component." p.44: "According to Manpung (1993), Tai-Khamti has nine tones. The five tones Tone1 to Tone5 may be marked as contrastive tones used in the vocabulary of the language; Short tone (Tone6) and Bass tone (Tone7) are used for prosodic purposes." p.45: "In a syllable consisting of a single front mid-vowel ә or, in an abbreviated word consisting of a consonant and a front mid-vowel CV(ә) resulting from consonant deletion, subdued pitch or DEPRESS tone is used (D superscript is marked for the depress tone). As for instance, [CV(ә)-CVC] → mәD – muŋ2 ‘mango’ ... Tone 2 Depress tone-symbol: Subdued pitch for abbreviated syllable"

new_statements.rule_in_words: Khamti is a syllable-tone language (five citation tones; every syllable, including each syllable of polysyllabic loans, carries a tone). No source states where word stress falls. The only prosodic asymmetry described is reduction of non-final syllables: the first element of disyllabic compounds may be 'abbreviated' to C+ə with a 'subdued pitch' (Manpoong's depress tone), and Morey (2005: 133, 196; 2005b: 166) reports that the revised Khamti script reserves a tone mark for 'unstressed syllables in polysyllabic loan words'. This implies full (tone-bearing) final syllables versus reducible pre-final syllables, but no author formulates a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords (Pali, Assamese, Burmese, English): every syllable receives a tone, mostly Tone 1 (Das p.54); Morey 2005: 133 reports for the closely related Phake that unstressed medial syllables of Pali loans take the level first tone and that the Khamti script has a special mark for such unstressed syllables. Weidert 1977: 28 notes 'toneless syllables' realised at mid pitch with relaxed vowel articulation.
new_statements.domain_note: All statements concern lexical/citation forms and the syllable as tone-bearing unit; Morey 2005: 81 explicitly says word/phrase-level prosodic (stress) analysis was not undertaken for the Tai languages of NE India. Das describes Indian Khamti (Chongkham, Arunachal Pradesh); Inglis 2014 (Myanmar Khamti) likewise says only 'tone with every syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Das 2014, Handique 2016, Borgohain 2019 and Borah 2020 describe Indian Tai-Khamti (Chongkham/Namsai area, Arunachal Pradesh, and Narayanpur, Assam); Inglis 2014 and Dockum 2017/2019 describe Khamti of Myanmar ('Khamti Shan', Chindwin/Putao). All fall under kham1290; Glottolog lists sub-dialects but none of the sources is keyed to a dialect glottocode, and the tone systems reported for India (Harris/Morey/Das) and Myanmar (Inglis) match (five tones).

new_statements.quote: p.287: "বৰ্তমান আমাৰ এই অধ্যয়নত আইতন আৰু খামতি ভাষা দুটাত প্ৰচলিত স্বৰ, ব্যঞ্জন আৰু সুৰৰ সাংবহনিক বিশ্লেষণত স্বৰৰ দৈৰ্ঘ্য, স্বৰৰ মৌলিক কম্পনাংক, স্বৰ আৰু ব্যঞ্জনৰ শক্তিবদ্ধ কম্পনাংক, ঘোষতাৰ সূচনা কাল আৰু সুৰৰ সুৰাঘাত দিশতহে বিশ্লেষণ কৰা হ'ল। বাকী স্বৰ আৰু ব্যঞ্জনৰ তীব্ৰতা, বাগ্‌ধ্বনিৰ শক্তি, ধ্বনিৰ সংক্ৰমণ আদি দিশৰ লগতে অক্ষৰ, শ্বাসাঘাত, সন্ধিৰ ক্ষেত্ৰত সাংবহনিক অধ্যয়ন বাদ পৰি ৰ'ল।" p.47: "খামতি ভাষা একাক্ষৰী আৰু সুৰীয়া ভাষা।" p.270: "খামতি ভাষাত এই সাতটা সুৰৰ প্ৰয়োগত প্ৰত্যেক শব্দৰ অৰ্থ সুকীয়া হৈছে। গতিকে খামতি ভাষাৰ সুৰক অবিভাজ্য বিশিষ্ট ধ্বনি বুলিব পাৰি।"
new_statements.translation: p.287: "In the present study the acoustic analysis of the vowels, consonants and tones current in the two languages Aiton and Khamti was carried out only with respect to vowel length, vowel fundamental frequency, vowel and consonant formants, voice onset time and the pitch of the tones. Acoustic study of the remaining aspects, such as the intensity of vowels and consonants, speech energy and transitions, together with the syllable, stress [শ্বাসাঘাত] and sandhi, was left out." p.47: "Khamti is a monosyllabic and tonal language." p.270: "In Khamti the meaning of each word is distinguished by the use of these seven tones. Hence the tones of Khamti can be called distinctive suprasegmental phonemes."

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Das 2014 (tone marks every syllable; no word-stress statement): a tone language with no placement statement. Borah adds an explicit disclaimer that stress was not studied (p. 287), so it supplies no placement rule and cannot refine the empty catalog rule. It describes the Khamti of Assam (Lakhimpur district) and Arunachal Pradesh (Namsai district), the same variety as Das 2014 and Handique 2016.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis treats Khamti as a monosyllabic, isolating, tonal language with seven contrastive tones on a syllable (rising, mid, falling, low-rising, mid-falling, glottalised, low; F0 tracks in Hz given for men, women, boys and girls, pp. 276-281). It makes no statement about where word stress falls or whether stress is contrastive; the conclusion says explicitly that stress (and the syllable and sandhi) was left out of the study. 'Stress' occurs otherwise only as a generic example of a suprasegmental in the definition of tone (sec. 0.11.11 p. 25 and sec. 6.2 p. 266) and in summaries of general phonetics handbooks in the literature review (pp. 2-3).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the thesis notes (p. 47, p. 269) that although Khamti is monosyllabic, diphthongs and consonant clusters occur, and that earlier authors (Needham, Grierson, S. N. Goswami, Bhimkanta Baruah, Prabin Saikia) counted between three and seven tones; the author's own fieldwork finds seven.
new_statements.identity_note: Borah 2020 describes the Khamti spoken in Assam (Lakhimpur district villages, table 1.1.4.1 p. 40, map 1.2.2(a) p. 33) and Namsai district, Arunachal Pradesh (map 1.2.2(b) p. 34), i.e. Indian Tai-Khamti, alongside Aiton; not the Chindwin/Myanmar Khamti of Inglis 2014 and Dockum 2017.

tone_statements.quote: KS has five tones as described by Harris (1976:114), aligning closely with Phake (Morey 2008:217). The tones are low falling /21/, mid falling /42/ and high falling /53/, mid rising /34/ and high level /55/. The low falling and high level tones exhibit allophonic variation—shorter duration with some glottal restriction and level pitch—for stop-final syllables and some open syllables with short vowels.
tone_statements.locator: p. xlviii, sec. 2 'Phoneme inventory of Khamti Shan (Myanmar)'; see also sec. 3.3 Tones + Table 5, pp. lii-liii
tone_statements.summary: Five tones on every syllable: low falling 21, mid rising 34, mid falling 42, high falling 53, high level 55; 21 and 55 short, glottalised in checked syllables; little tone sandhi; nothing on stress.

II (pp. 31-55) covers consonants, vowels, five citation tones, syllable structure and morphophonology. p.53: every syllable is marked by tone; loanwords get a tone on every syllable (mostly Tone 1). p.45 (after Manpung 1993): 'Depress tone: subdued pitch for abbreviated syllable' -- reduced CV(ə) first syllables of compounds (məD-muŋ2 'mango') take a subdued pitch. The word 'stress' is never applied to Khamti; no statement of where word stress falls. Variety: Tai-Khamti of Chongkham/Namsai, Lohit district, Arunachal Pradesh.

tone.summary: Five syllable tones: low falling 21, mid rising 34, mid falling 42, high falling 53, high level 55; checked syllables take short low/high allophones; little tone sandhi; nothing said on word stress.

sources.note: Per search summary of the academia.edu text: reports 2014 fieldwork in the Chindwin River valley (Khamti District, Burma); finds 'a significantly different tonal system.. with just four lexical tonemes instead of the five described in India'; argues the mismatch between tonal and segmental evidence can be resolved with the comparative method and presents Khamti as a case study in the utility of tonal evidence for subgrouping within Southwestern Tai (Chamberlain 1975 vs Edmondson and Solnit 1997 vs Luo 2001).
